title: Pullback to the Moving Averages
teaches: The pullback to the moving averages as we trade it: a leader in a stacked, rising trend drifts quietly onto a rising 10-day or 50-day, a session closes at or above the line, the buy is a market order as price trades over that session's high, the stop sits a few cents under the pullback low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

questions.q: A pullback buy in this setup sits on which kind of line?
choices: A rising line in an uptrend
A falling line, to buy the bounce
A flat line inside a range
Any line the stock touched
questions.answer: A rising line in an uptrend
questions.why: A rising line in an uptrend. The card wants the line higher than it was 10 sessions ago. A line that has stopped rising takes the pullback off the list. Touching a rising line is not enough on its own.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the dip onto a line that is rising, never one that is flat or falling.

wrong.A falling line, to buy the bounce: A falling line is a downtrend. The card wants the line higher than 10 sessions ago.
wrong.A flat line inside a range: A flat line is a warning. The card says the line must be rising.
wrong.Any line the stock touched: Any line is how we end up buying a random average. The line must be rising.

questions.simple: We buy a dip only onto a line that is still rising, because a line that stopped rising is off the list.

reasons: the 10-session rising test is a proposed card number (map.line_rising)

questions.q: For a pullback buy, price is above the 200-day and the 20 EMA is above the 50 above the 200.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The close sits above the 200-day SMA, and the 20 EMA sits above the 50 SMA, which sits above the 200 SMA. That is the stacked trend a pullback buy needs. Passing the stack does not make the stock a buy.
questions.lesson_line: Stack the averages: 20 EMA over the 50-day over the 200-day, with price above the 200-day.
questions.simple: True, because we want price over the 200-day and the 20 EMA over the 50-day over the 200-day.

deeper.trap: Price above the 200-day is only half of it. A stock can sit over the 200-day with the 20 EMA still under the 50, and that fails the stack the card asks for.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, no longs below the 200-day) and the 200-day decision D-009 is held
the 50-over-200 order is the card's rule, not B26

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The stop sits a few ___ under the low, not exactly on it.
questions.answer: cents
questions.why: Cents. The stop sits a few cents under the low, not exactly on it. Stop first: the size comes from the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the low.
questions.simple: A few cents. The stop sits just under the low, not exactly on it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F62, A3)
which low the stop sits under is held as D-008, so the question keys only 'a few cents'

questions.q: The hold day is done and price trades over its high. How do we buy?
choices: A market order, in regular hours
A limit order at the hold day's high
A stop-limit order after the close
A market order at tomorrow's open
questions.answer: A market order, in regular hours
questions.why: A market order, in regular hours. Entries are market orders, placed the moment the trigger trades. A limit order at the high can miss the move. An order placed after the close, or at tomorrow's open, is not the rule.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger trades, you buy at market, and the stop goes in right away.

wrong.A limit order at the hold day's high: Entries are market orders. A limit order at the high can sit unfilled while the stock leaves.
wrong.A stop-limit order after the close: The rule is a market order the moment the trigger trades, in regular hours.
wrong.A market order at tomorrow's open: We do not wait for tomorrow. The rule is a market order the moment the trigger trades.

questions.simple: We buy at market the moment price trades over the hold day's high, during regular hours.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, market orders)
the buy trigger itself is held as D-003 and is not graded

questions.q: A pullback buy is for leaders: an RS rating of 60 or more, in one of the strongest groups.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. We buy leaders, with an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. The pullback card asks for the same: 80 or more, in a strong group. A weak stock dipping to a line is not the same trade.
questions.lesson_line: Pullbacks are for leaders: RS rating 80 or more. A weak stock dipping to a line is not the same trade.
questions.simple: False. The card asks for an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group, and 60 is too low.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)
when RS is read is held as D-011 and is never asked

questions.q: How many entries and stops does one pullback trade have?
choices: One entry, then add on each dip
Two halves, two prices, two stops
One entry, one price, one stop
One entry, stop lowered if it dips
questions.answer: One entry, one price, one stop
questions.why: One entry at one price with one stop. The full size goes in at once, with no adds and no second buy lower. That holds even if the stock dips back to the line and holds.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop, full size. No adding to a pullback buy.

wrong.One entry, then add on each dip: No adds. A second buy lower is ruled out.
wrong.Two halves, two prices, two stops: The full size goes in at one price with one stop.
wrong.One entry, stop lowered if it dips: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.

questions.simple: One buy at one price with one stop. We never add to it, even on a dip.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, adds settled as D-135)

questions.q: On the card, what does a healthy pullback look like on volume?
choices: Heavy: well above the 50-day average
Rising a bit more on each down day
Volume is not part of the card
Quiet: below the 50-day average
questions.answer: Quiet: below the 50-day average
questions.why: Quiet. On our card, the average volume over the pullback days sits below the 50-day average. The touch day is not above 1.5 times it. Minervini's template also looks for low volume during pullbacks. Volume rising on the pullback is a B- cue. Quiet volume is one check, not a buy signal.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet volume on the dip is the picture. Heavy volume under the line is not.

wrong.Heavy: well above the 50-day average: Heavy selling into the line is a warning, not a pullback.
wrong.Rising a bit more on each down day: Volume rising on the pullback is a B- cue on our card.
wrong.Volume is not part of the card: It is on the card as a check and a grade cue, and a heavy close under the line is an invalidation.

questions.simple: A healthy pullback drifts down on quiet volume, below the 50-day average. Heavy selling into the line is a warning.

reasons: +2 proposed card criterion (map.volume); the research scan found quiet volume made little difference

questions.q: A pullback low that dips 0.5 ATR under the line can still count as a touch.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The touch is a pullback low within 1 ATR under to 0.25 ATR over the line. So 0.5 ATR under is inside that range. Moving averages give no exact support or resistance levels. A touch alone is not a buy: the hold day must still close at or above the line.
questions.lesson_line: The touch is a band around the line, not one exact price.
questions.simple: True, because the touch is a zone around the line, not one exact price, and 0.5 ATR under sits inside it.

reasons: the touch range of 1 ATR under to 0.25 ATR over is a proposed card number (map.touch)

questions.q: How deep must the dip be to count as a pullback?
choices: Close 1 ATR under the 11-day high
A close 1% under the 11-day high
Down 25% from the 52-week high
Any red day at all counts as a dip
questions.answer: Close 1 ATR under the 11-day high
questions.why: A close at least 1 ATR under the highest high of the last 11 sessions. One ATR is the minimum depth. The card measures the dip in ATR. The 25% figure is a different check: price within 25% of its 52-week high on the hold day.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the dip in ATR from the recent high. One ATR is the minimum.

wrong.A close 1% under the 11-day high: The card measures the dip in ATR, not a fixed percent. It wants a close at least 1 ATR under the high.
wrong.Down 25% from the 52-week high: That is the trend filter, not the dip depth. Price must be within 25% of its 52-week high on the hold day.
wrong.Any red day at all counts as a dip: One red day is not a pullback. The card wants a close at least 1 ATR under the high.

questions.simple: A pullback must close at least 1 ATR under the recent high, so one small red day does not count.

reasons: the 1 ATR minimum and the 11-session window are proposed card numbers (map.depth)

questions.q: On this card, how long does the pullback last, swing high to touch day?
choices: 1 session
2 to 8 sessions
10 to 15 sessions
30 or more sessions
questions.answer: 2 to 8 sessions
questions.why: 2 to 8 sessions from the swing high to the touch day. One session is below the 2 session minimum. Anything past 8 is longer than this card allows. On the 20 EMA, the 20 EMA Pullback card has its own 2 to 15 window.
questions.lesson_line: Two to eight sessions of drift. One day is a drop, not a drift.

wrong.1 session: The minimum is 2 sessions. A one-day drop is below it.
wrong.10 to 15 sessions: That is longer than this card allows. On the 20 EMA, a drift that long is judged on the 20 EMA Pullback card.
wrong.30 or more sessions: That is far past the 8 session limit on this card.

questions.simple: This card wants a pullback of 2 to 8 sessions from the swing high to the touch day.

reasons: the 2 to 8 session length is a proposed card number (map.length)

questions.q: A pullback can include one down day larger than 3 ATR and still be called orderly.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Orderly means no single down day larger than 2 ATR in the pullback. A 3 ATR down day is over that limit. One outsized red day is also a B- cue on our card.
questions.lesson_line: Orderly means no single down day larger than 2 ATR.
questions.simple: False, because an orderly pullback has no single down day larger than 2 ATR, and 3 ATR is bigger than that.

reasons: the 2 ATR down-day limit is a proposed card number (map.orderly)

questions.q: What makes a session the hold day?
choices: It trades the highest volume of the dip
It closes below the line by 1 ATR
Its close is at or above the line
Its low never dips under the line
questions.answer: Its close is at or above the line
questions.why: The touch day closes at or above the line, and that close is the hold. If the low undercuts the line, the next day's close at or above it can be the hold instead. Volume does not name the hold day. A close under the line is not a hold.
questions.lesson_line: A hold is a close at or above the line. Then wait for the trigger.

wrong.It trades the highest volume of the dip: Volume does not name the hold day. The close against the line does.
wrong.It closes below the line by 1 ATR: A close under the line is not a hold. The hold is a close at or above it.
wrong.Its low never dips under the line: The low may dip a little under the line. The close at or above it is what counts.

questions.simple: The hold day is the session that closes at or above the line. The close decides it, not the volume.

reasons: +2 ties to the held trigger decision D-003 (the buy follows the hold day)

questions.q: In an Orange market we take A+ setups only.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The market reading sets the risk before the chart does. Green is full risk, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange A+ only, Red mostly cash and shorts. Orange limits which setups we take. It is not a ban on trading.
questions.lesson_line: The market reading sets how much and which setups. Orange means A+ only.
questions.simple: In an Orange market we only take the best setups, the A+ ones, because the market reading sets the risk.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (F65)

questions.q: What is the minimum price and daily traded value?
choices: $10 and $5 million a day
$20 and $100 million a day
No minimum if RS is 90
$10 and $20 million a day
questions.answer: $10 and $20 million a day
questions.why: $10 and $20 million a day. We trade only stocks priced at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. A strong RS rating does not remove the floor.
questions.lesson_line: Price $10 or more and $20 million or more traded a day. Thinner names are skipped.

wrong.$20 and $100 million a day: That is stricter than the rule. The floor is $10 and $20 million a day.
wrong.No minimum if RS is 90: Strong RS does not remove the liquidity floor.
wrong.$10 and $5 million a day: The price floor is right but the volume floor is too low. It is $20 million a day.

questions.simple: We only trade stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. Thinner names are skipped.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (B23 price and volume floor)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A gap against the stop: the first ___-minute low is the new stop.
questions.why: 30. After a gap against the stop, the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low decides.
questions.simple: The first 30 minutes of the gap day decide, and the low of that first 30-minute bar is the new stop.

reasons: the key rests on one cited fact (B20)
rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: Bought at 86.93 with the stop at 85.82. One R is the buy minus the stop. Where is 3R?
questions.why: One R is the buy minus the stop: 86.93 minus 85.82. Add three of those to the buy of 86.93 to get 90.26. That is the 3R mark, a yardstick and not a fixed sale.
questions.lesson_line: 3R is the buy plus three R. It is a yardstick, not a sell order.
questions.simple: 3R is 90.26, which is the buy plus three times the gap between the buy and the stop.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, a third at 3R)
the buy trigger behind the example is held as D-003

wrong.$89.15: Added the three R to the stop, not to the buy.
wrong.$91.37: Counted four R instead of three.

questions.q: Is today the hold day?
choices: No, the low must stay above the line
No, it needs a second close above
Yes, it closed at or above the line
questions.answer: Yes, it closed at or above the line
questions.why: Yes. The touch day closed at or above the line, which makes it the hold day. Now wait for the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: One close at or above the line is the hold. The buy comes next, on the trigger.

wrong.No, the low must stay above the line: The low may touch or dip a little. The close is what counts.
wrong.No, it needs a second close above: One close at or above the line is the hold.

questions.story: A leader drifts four quiet days onto its rising 10-day. Today the low touched the line and it closed above it.

questions.q: Bought at 64.00 with the stop at 61.50. How far under the buy is the stop, in percent, to one decimal?
questions.why: The gap is 64.00 minus 61.50. Divide it by the buy of 64.00, not the stop, to get 3.9%. That is wider than the usual limit of about 3%.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop in percent of the buy. Over about 3% is wider than we usually allow.
questions.simple: The stop is 3.9 percent under the buy, which is over our usual 3 percent.

deeper.trap: Divide the gap by the buy price, not by the stop. The 3% limit is measured against the buy.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A13, about 3%)

wrong.4.1%: Divided by the stop instead of the buy.
wrong.2.5%: Read the dollar gap as a percent.

questions.q: A stock 30% under its 52-week high still passes the trend filter for a pullback buy.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Price must be within 25% of its 52-week high on the hold day, and 30% under is outside it. Minervini's template, as Deepvue writes it, uses the same 25%. It is one trend check of many, not a buy signal.
questions.lesson_line: Stay within 25% of the 52-week high. A deeper hole is a recovery.
questions.simple: False, because the card wants price within 25% of its 52-week high, and 30% under is outside that.

deeper.trap: Do not read the 25% as a buy signal. It is one trend check. A stock can sit well inside 25% of its high and still fail the line, depth or length checks.

reasons: the 25% limit is a proposed card number (map.near_high), though Deepvue's Minervini page agrees

questions.q: What usually comes before a pullback worth buying?
choices: A long sleep under the 200-day
A breakout, earnings gap or up-cycle
A month falling on heavy volume
No prior run; a rising line
questions.answer: A breakout, earnings gap or up-cycle
questions.why: A breakout, an earnings gap or a new up-cycle within the last 3 months (63 sessions) comes before the pullback. The dip needs a run to dip from. Bonde's list of common pullback methods includes buying the first pullback after a major breakout. A catalyst alone is not a buy, because the rest of the card must pass too.
questions.lesson_line: A pullback needs something to pull back from: a breakout, a gap, a new up-cycle.

wrong.A long sleep under the 200-day: A stock asleep under the 200-day is not a leader in an uptrend.
wrong.A month falling on heavy volume: Heavy selling is distribution, not a leader's rest.
wrong.No prior run; a rising line: A dip needs a run to dip from. The card wants a breakout, gap or new up-cycle first. Bonde: buy the first pullback after a major breakout.

questions.simple: A pullback needs a recent breakout, earnings gap or new up-cycle to pull back from, within the last 3 months.

reasons: +2 proposed card criterion (map.recent_catalyst), the Bonde line is one trader's list

questions.q: A buy hits 3R on its first day. What does our plan say about selling?
choices: Sell a third now; 3R is the rule
Sell half now and lock the gain
Judge it; he rarely sells on day 1
Sell it all before the close
questions.answer: Judge it; he rarely sells on day 1
questions.why: Judge it. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. He very rarely sells on day 1 of the buy and usually waits until day 3 at the earliest.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment. Rarely day 1, often day 3 or later.

wrong.Sell a third now; 3R is the rule: 3R is no fixed sell point. The first sell is a judgment.
wrong.Sell half now and lock the gain: He very rarely sells on day 1 of the buy.
wrong.Sell it all before the close: He very rarely sells on day 1 of the buy.

questions.simple: No fixed sale at 3R. The first sell is a judgment, and he rarely sells on day 1.

deeper.trap: Treating 3R as a sell signal. It is a yardstick. He often sells into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (B19: a third at 3R, breakeven 2R to 5R, default at the first trim)

questions.q: A steadier mover's last third is trailed under the 21-day and sold on a close below it.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The default trail is the 10-day for fast movers and the 21-day for steadier ones. Either way it is sold on a close below the line.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 10-day trail. Steadier, 21-day. Sell on a close below.
questions.simple: True. A steadier mover's last third rides under the 21-day and is sold on a close below it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (E52: the trail line depends on how fast the stock moves)

questions.q: Do we buy the break?
choices: Yes, the chart looks very clean
Yes, but with half the size
No; a report is within 3 days
No; it needs a second close above
questions.answer: No; a report is within 3 days
questions.why: No. We take no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. A report in 2 sessions is inside that window. Hold through a report only if the trade is already up 5R. A clean chart or half size does not change that.
questions.lesson_line: Three days before a report, no new buy. Check the date first.

wrong.Yes, the chart looks very clean: A good chart does not move the rule. No new buys in the 3 days before a report.
wrong.Yes, but with half the size: Half size does not fix it. The rule is no new buy inside the window.
wrong.No; it needs a second close above: One close at or above the line is the hold. The reason to pass is the report, not a missing second close.

questions.story: The hold day just printed. The stock reports earnings in 2 sessions. Tomorrow it may trade over today's high.
questions.simple: No. We do not open a new buy in the 3 days before an earnings report, however clean the chart looks.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (B22 earnings window)

questions.q: The 52-week high is 300.00. The stock closed at 238.00 on the hold day. How far under the high is the close, as a percent of the high?
questions.why: The drop is 300.00 minus 238.00. Divide it by the high of 300.00 to get 20.7%. That is inside the 25% limit on the hold day, so the trend filter passes. It is one check of many, not a buy.
questions.lesson_line: Percent off the high is a quick filter. Under 25% passes it.
questions.simple: The stock is 20.7% under its high, which is inside the 25% limit, so it passes the trend filter.

reasons: +2 computed key (percent under the high)

wrong.26.1%: Divided the drop by the close instead of the high.
wrong.79.3%: Found where the close sits as a share of the high, not the drop.

questions.q: What does the plan do at 186?
choices: Nothing new; the first stop decides
Buy more to lower the average cost
Move the stop down under the new low
Sell half now to cut the risk
questions.answer: Nothing new; the first stop decides
questions.why: Nothing new. The plan is one entry at one price with one stop, with no adds and no second buy lower. The first stop is the exit, and it only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Do not add on a dip. The first stop still decides.

wrong.Buy more to lower the average cost: Averaging down is not ours. A second buy lower is ruled out.
wrong.Move the stop down under the new low: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Sell half now to cut the risk: The plan trims a third at 3R, not half on a dip.

questions.story: You bought the 50-day hold at 190. The stock dips to 186 and holds the line again.
questions.simple: We do not add on a dip. One buy, one stop, and the first stop stays the exit.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (A4, A5, adds settled as D-135)

questions.q: The 50-day is 410.00 and ATR is 9.00. The pullback low was 400.10. How many ATR under the line did it dip?
questions.answer: 1.10 ATR
questions.why: The dip under the line is 410.00 minus 400.10. Divide it by the 9.00 ATR to get 1.10. The touch rule allows a low from 1 ATR under to 0.25 ATR over the line. So 1.1 ATR under is outside it, not a touch.
questions.lesson_line: Divide the dip under the line by ATR. More than 1 ATR under is not a touch.
questions.simple: The low dipped 1.1 ATR under the line, which is past the 1 ATR limit, so it is not a touch.

reasons: the key rests on one cited fact (the touch rule)
computed key
the touch rule is a card proposal, not settled

choices: 9.90 ATR
1.10 ATR
0.91 ATR
0.02 ATR

wrong.9.90 ATR: Never divided the dip by the ATR.
wrong.0.91 ATR: Flipped the division: ATR over the dip.
wrong.0.02 ATR: Divided the dip by the line price instead of the ATR.

questions.q: Wait for tomorrow's reclaim, or drop it?
choices: Wait; one close proves nothing
Drop it; that is distribution
Buy now to catch the low
questions.answer: Drop it; that is distribution
questions.why: Drop it. A close under the line on more than 1.5 times the 50-day volume is distribution, not a pullback.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume under the line is selling. It is not a pullback to buy.

wrong.Wait; one close proves nothing: A close under the line on more than 1.5 times the 50-day volume is distribution.
wrong.Buy now to catch the low: Buying into heavy selling under the line is the mistake.

questions.story: On day five of a pullback, the stock closes under its 10-day on 2.3 times its 50-day average volume.

questions.q: If the honest stop is 3.6% wide, tighten it to 3% and keep the full size.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. When the honest stop is more than about 3% under the entry, the size comes down. That keeps the account risk the same. Never move the stop up to make it fit. If even the smaller size does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: A wide stop shrinks the size. It never gets tightened to fit.
questions.simple: False. A wide stop means a smaller size, never a tighter stop just to make it fit.

deeper.trap: The honest stop is the real exit. Moving it to 3% changes the picture on paper, not the stock. The honest stop is still 3.6% away, and the full size still risks more than the plan allows.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (A3, A13)

questions.q: Which of these is the stop mistake on this setup?
choices: A few cents under the low
A stop order with the broker
Line minus a cushion, at full size
The stop only moves up
questions.answer: Line minus a cushion, at full size
questions.why: The line minus a cushion, at full size. That puts the stop far wider than 3% while the size stays the same, so the real risk is bigger than planned. The plan puts the stop a few cents under the low. It is a real order with the broker, and it only moves up. The size comes down when the stop runs wider.
questions.lesson_line: Stop a few cents under the low. Not under the line minus a cushion.

wrong.A few cents under the low: That is the plan. The stop sits a few cents under the low, not exactly on it.
wrong.A stop order with the broker: A real stop order with the broker is required.
wrong.The stop only moves up: That is the plan. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up.

questions.simple: The mistake is a stop set under the line minus a cushion while keeping full size. The other three are the plan.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (A3, A13, D41)

questions.q: Every trade sells a fixed third at 3R, then a third at 5R.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. He rarely sells on day 1 and often waits for a 3, 5 or 7 day push.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment. Often day 3 or later, into a push.
questions.simple: False. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (E51)

questions.q: A pullback that gaps 5% over the trigger price is still fine to buy at the open.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Skip if the fill would be more than 4% above the trigger price, and a 5% gap is past that. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Chasing the bounce day is a listed mistake on the card.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% past the trigger, skip it. No chasing.
questions.simple: False. A fill more than 4% above the trigger is a chase, so we skip it.

deeper.counter: A fill up to 4% above the trigger is not a skip. But the stop still sits under the pullback low, so the stop is now wider in percent. If it runs past our limit for a stop, the size comes down.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (C28, the 4% limit)

questions.q: The trigger is 31.80. What is the highest fill we accept, with the 4% rule?
questions.why: Four percent is added to the trigger: 31.80 times 1.04 is 33.07. A fill above that is more than 4% over the trigger, so we skip it. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
questions.lesson_line: Work out your chase ceiling before the open.
questions.simple: The highest fill is 33.07, which is the trigger of 31.80 plus 4 percent.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, 4% chase limit)

wrong.$30.53: Took 4% off the trigger instead of adding it.
wrong.$35.80: Added four dollars instead of four percent.
wrong.$31.93: Slipped a decimal and added only a tenth of the 4%.

questions.q: Account 50,000, risk 1%, buy 31.80, stop 30.67. Risk dollars divided by the stop distance: how many shares, rounded down?
questions.answer: 442 shares
questions.why: Risk dollars are 1% of 50,000. The stop distance is 31.80 minus 30.67. Divide the risk dollars by that distance and round down to 442 shares. The wider the stop, the fewer shares.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. Account times risk, divided by the stop distance.
questions.simple: You can buy 442 shares, because the dollars at risk are split by the stop distance and rounded down.

deeper.trap: Round down, never up. Rounding the result up would risk a little more than the 1% you set. The stop sets the size, so a wider stop means fewer shares for the same risk.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A3)

choices: 15 shares
4,424 shares
44,247 shares
442 shares

wrong.15 shares: Divided the risk dollars by the buy price, not the stop distance.
wrong.4,424 shares: Slipped a decimal and risked ten times too much.
wrong.44,247 shares: Used the whole account as the risk dollars.

questions.q: Pullback or Remount?

Pullback; the 50-day held in the end
Pullback; big volume backs the bounce
Undercut and Rally; it broke the line

questions.lesson_line: Count the closes under the line. Two at most is a pullback.

wrong.Pullback; the 50-day held in the end: A pullback allows at most two closes under the line. Seven is a lost line.
wrong.Pullback; big volume backs the bounce: Volume does not change the count of closes under the line.
wrong.Undercut and Rally; it broke the line: The count decides it. Five or more consecutive closes under the line, one 0.5 ATR under, is a Remount.

questions.story: The stock closed under its 50-day for seven sessions in a row, one close more than 0.5 ATR under it. Today it closed back above it on big volume.
questions.simple: It is a Remount: seven closes under the 50-day is far past the two a pullback allows.

deeper.trap: Count the closes. At most two under the line is a pullback. Five or more, with one 0.5 ATR under, is a Remount. Big volume on the bounce does not change the count.

questions.q: Which card does this belong to?
choices: This card, the 10-day form
This card, the 50-day form
The Remount card, a line lost
The 20 EMA Pullback card

questions.story: A leader's low tags its 20 EMA and the stock holds above its 50-day. The 200-day sits far below.
questions.simple: A low that tags the 20 EMA and holds above the 50-day belongs to the 20 EMA Pullback card, not this one.

questions.q: Pullback or Undercut and Rally?
choices: Pullback; the line held by the close
Neither; the line broke, so we skip it
Remount; a line lost and retaken
Undercut and Rally; buy the reclaim
questions.answer: Undercut and Rally; buy the reclaim
questions.why: Undercut and Rally. A buy taken as price trades back above a broken line is the Undercut and Rally, not a pullback. A pullback buys over the hold day's high after a close at or above the line. This lesson names the setup by the buy and sets no depth for an undercut.
questions.lesson_line: The buy names the setup. Over the hold day's high is a pullback.

wrong.Pullback; the line held by the close: A pullback buys over the hold day's high. This buy is the move back above a broken line.
wrong.Neither; the line broke, so we skip it: The break and reclaim is a named setup of its own, the Undercut and Rally.
wrong.Remount; a line lost and retaken: A Remount needs five or more consecutive closes under the line. This broke and came back in one day.

questions.story: At 10 am a leader's low breaks 1% under its 50-day. By noon price is back above the line, and you buy the move back through.
questions.simple: Buying the move back above a line that just broke is the Undercut and Rally, not a pullback.

deeper.trap: The same intraday dip can be a pullback. If the day closes at or above the line, the buy waits for price to trade over that day's high. That is a pullback. The setup is named by when and how you buy.

+2 rests on the card's lookalike tell, which can change

questions.q: Pullback or EMA Crossback?
choices: EMA Crossback; the up-cycle is new
Pullback; it is touching the lines
Remount; the stock lost its lines
Undercut and Rally; it lost the lines
questions.answer: EMA Crossback; the up-cycle is new
questions.why: EMA Crossback. Count from the close back above the 9 and 20 EMA out of a decline. After a Wedge Pop, the stock tests its moving averages, forming an EMA Crossback. A later touch of a line that has been rising for months is the pullback. A Remount is five or more closes under the 50-day or 200-day, then a retake.
questions.lesson_line: A test right after the new up-cycle is a Crossback. A later one is a pullback.

wrong.Remount; the stock lost its lines: A Remount is a 50-day or 200-day lost for five or more closes and retaken. Today is a test of the 9 and 20 EMA.
wrong.Pullback; it is touching the lines: A touch right after a new up-cycle is the Crossback. A later touch of a long-rising line is the pullback.
wrong.Undercut and Rally; it lost the lines: That needs a low that broke under the line and a buy as price trades back above it. Nothing broke today.

questions.story: Six sessions ago a stock closed back above its 9 and 20 EMA after a correction. Today it touches them for the first time.
questions.simple: A first test of the averages soon after a new up-cycle is an EMA Crossback. A later touch of a long-rising line is a pullback.

deeper.counter: Same stock, months later. The 20 EMA has been rising for months and price dips to it for the first time in that run. That is the pullback to the moving averages, not the Crossback. What differs is how long the line has been rising.

reasons: +2 held decision D-026 (how touches are counted)
+2 the Crossback wording comes from a vendor summary of Kell, beside the card's tell

questions.q: Pullback to the averages, or Bull Flag?
choices: Pullback; it touched the 10 EMA
Bull Flag; a fast gain came first
Pullback; four days is too short
Remount; it fell to the 10 EMA
questions.answer: Bull Flag; a fast gain came first
questions.why: Bull Flag. A bull flag needs a 20% or larger gain inside 20 sessions, and 28% in 9 sessions is that pole. A pullback to the averages needs no pole. It needs a rising line in a stacked trend and a 1 ATR dip from the swing high to the line.
questions.lesson_line: A big, fast pole before a tight drift means a flag. No pole means a pullback.

wrong.Pullback; it touched the 10 EMA: A pullback needs no pole. A 28% gain in 9 sessions is a bull flag's pole.
wrong.Pullback; four days is too short: Length is not what decides it. The pole is.
wrong.Remount; it fell to the 10 EMA: A Remount is five or more closes under the 50-day or 200-day. This drift was 4 tight days onto the 10 EMA.

questions.story: A stock gains 28% in 9 sessions, then drifts 4 tight days down onto its 10 EMA.
questions.simple: It is a bull flag, because the 28% gain in 9 sessions is a pole and a plain pullback needs no pole.

deeper.trap: The pole decides the name. Take the same 4 tight days onto the 10 EMA with no 20% gain in the 20 sessions before. It can then be a pullback to the averages, if the line is rising and the dip is at least 1 ATR.

reasons: the 20% in 20 sessions pole test is a proposed card number
the key rests on the card's own lookalike tell

questions.q: Is this a pullback to buy?
choices: Yes, any touch of the 50-day works
Yes, if volume stays quiet
No, the 50-day is no longer rising
No, a drifting leader is a broken one
questions.answer: No, the 50-day is no longer rising
questions.why: No. The line must be rising, higher than its value 10 sessions ago, and here the 50-day is lower. A line that stops rising takes the pullback off the list before entry. Quiet volume or a bare touch does not fix that.
questions.lesson_line: A flat or falling line is not support. Skip it.

wrong.Yes, any touch of the 50-day works: The line must be rising. Buying the touch just because it is the line is the mistake.
wrong.Yes, if volume stays quiet: Quiet volume does not fix a falling line.
wrong.No, a drifting leader is a broken one: A pullback is a short drift down onto a line, so drifting alone is not the problem. The line has stopped rising, and that is.

questions.story: A leader drifts down onto its 50-day. Today the 50-day reads 142.10. Ten sessions ago it read 143.40.
questions.simple: No, because a pullback buy needs a rising line, and this 50-day is lower than it was 10 sessions ago.

reasons: the 10-session rising test is a proposed card number (map.line_rising)

questions.q: What does our card say to do now?
choices: Wait until the index is back above
Buy; the stock is what matters
Wait for the index to make a new high
Wait for the stock to make a new high
questions.answer: Wait until the index is back above
questions.why: Wait. Before entry, if the index loses its 20-day, we stay patient until it is back above.
questions.lesson_line: A strong stock in a weak index still has to wait.

wrong.Buy; the stock is what matters: The card waits on the index too. When the index loses its 20-day, we stay patient.
wrong.Wait for the index to make a new high: The card waits for the index to get back above its 20-day, not for a new high.
wrong.Wait for the stock to make a new high: The card waits on the index, not the stock. The stock already passes every check.

questions.story: Your leader passes every check and trades over the hold day's high. The index just closed under its 20-day for the first time in weeks.
questions.simple: Wait, because when the index loses its 20-day, our card says to stay patient until it is back above.

reasons: the index 20-day waiting rule is a proposed card criterion (map.inv_index)

questions.q: Which one is orderly?
choices: The first; no one day is a spike
The second; a fast drop is OK
Both; each reaches the 50-day
Neither; six days is too long
questions.answer: The first; no one day is a spike
questions.why: The first. Orderly means no single down day larger than 2 ATR, and the first has none. The 2.5 ATR bars in the second fail it. A sharp 1 to 2 day drop into the line is also a B- cue on our card.
questions.lesson_line: Orderly means no down day larger than 2 ATR. A sharp drop is not orderly.

wrong.The second; a fast drop is OK: Orderly means no single down day larger than 2 ATR. The 2.5 ATR bars break it.
wrong.Both; each reaches the 50-day: A 2.5 ATR red bar breaks the 2 ATR limit, so the second is not orderly.
wrong.Neither; six days is too long: Six sessions fits the 2 to 8 session length. A drift with no outsized day breaks no rule here.

questions.story: Two pullbacks reach a rising 50-day. The first drifts six days, and its biggest down day is 0.8 ATR. The second drops on two days of 2.5 ATR red bars.
questions.simple: The first drift is orderly because its biggest down day is 0.8 ATR, under the 2 ATR limit.

reasons: the 2 ATR down-day limit is a proposed card number (map.orderly)

questions.q: What does that do to the grade and the size?
choices: Nothing; the grade and size stay
Tighten the stop to 3%
It grades down and the size shrinks

questions.story: A fast leader holds its 10-day. The pullback low sits 3.6% under your fill.

Yes, but only with a tighter stop
No, Orange means we stay in cash

questions.q: Which one is the cleaner pullback?
choices: The one with rising volume
The five days at 0.6x volume
They are equal on quality
Neither; 0.6x shows no buyers
questions.answer: The five days at 0.6x volume
questions.why: The five days at 0.6x. Pullback days at or under about 0.7x the 50-day average over 3 to 8 orderly sessions are an A+ cue. Volume rising on the pullback is a B- cue. These are cues for a judgment grade, not a fixed formula.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet is better than rising volume on the way down.

wrong.The one with rising volume: Volume rising on the pullback is a B- cue.
wrong.They are equal on quality: The card grades quiet volume higher than rising volume.
wrong.Neither; 0.6x shows no buyers: Quiet volume on the dip is the card's A+ cue, so 0.6x does not count against it.

questions.story: Two dips onto a rising 50-day. One runs five days at 0.6x the 50-day volume. The other has volume rising each day.
questions.simple: Quiet pullback volume, at or under about 0.7x the 50-day average, is an A+ cue. Rising volume is a B- cue.

questions.q: Does the reversal help the grade?
choices: Yes, a tight reversal at the line helps
Yes, since a hammer predicts a bounce
No, it helps the entry, not the grade
No, volume sets the grade, not candles
questions.answer: Yes, a tight reversal at the line helps
questions.why: Yes. A tight reversal at the line is an A+ cue, because it keeps the stop at 3% or less. A hammer, an inside day and an undercut and reclaim all count. It is a cue, not a guarantee. Grading is discretionary and hard to define.
questions.lesson_line: A tight reversal at the line keeps the stop small.

wrong.Yes, since a hammer predicts a bounce: A hammer is a cue, not a prediction. It helps because it keeps the stop at 3% or less.
wrong.No, it helps the entry, not the grade: Our card lists a tight reversal at the line as an A+ cue, so it does help the grade.
wrong.No, volume sets the grade, not candles: Quiet volume is one cue. A tight reversal at the line is another.

questions.story: A leader dips to its 10-day. The hold day is a hammer that closes on the line.
questions.simple: Yes, a tight reversal at the line is an A+ cue, because it keeps the stop at 3 percent or less.

deeper.trap: A hammer alone is not a buy signal. On our card the reversal helps the grade because it keeps the stop at 3% or less. Grading stays a judgment call, so no single candle makes a setup an A+.

grading is the owner's discretionary call (E50)

questions.q: What do we do about this stop?
choices: Cut the size, keep the same risk
Raise the risk to keep full size
Skip it; the stop is over our 3% limit
Keep full size; it is close enough
questions.answer: Cut the size, keep the same risk
questions.why: Cut the size so the account risk stays the same. The stop is 3.6% under the buy, wider than our usual 3%, so fewer shares fit the same risk. We never tighten the stop to make it fit. Skip only if even the smaller size does not fit.
questions.lesson_line: Wide stop on a fast leader: smaller size, same risk.

wrong.Raise the risk to keep full size: The size comes down so the account risk is unchanged. Risk does not go up to keep the size.
wrong.Skip it; the stop is over our 3% limit: A stop over about 3% means a smaller size. Skip only if even the smaller size does not fit.
wrong.Keep full size; it is close enough: Over about 3%, the size comes down so the account risk is unchanged.

questions.story: YELP, 2013. A fast leader that rode its 10 EMA since February drifts four quiet days. You plan to buy at 31.80 with the stop at 30.67.
questions.simple: Cut the size, because a stop wider than 3 percent means fewer shares for the same account risk.

deeper.trap: The trap is tightening the stop to 3% so the full size fits. That is no longer the honest stop at the pullback low. Before the buy the chart sets the stop. After the buy it only moves up. The size does the adjusting.

questions.q: Which line was this pullback, and is it ours?
choices: The 200-day; it is the base
The 50-day; yes, the deeper form
The 10-day; this is a fast leader
questions.answer: The 50-day; yes, the deeper form
questions.why: The 50-day, the deeper form. A mega cap's first test of the rising 50 SMA, six days on quiet volume, reached 3R in 10 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: The deeper pullback goes to the rising 50-day, in a leader.

wrong.The 200-day; it is the base: The 200-day is context, not the line this card buys.
wrong.The 10-day; this is a fast leader: The stock tested the 50-day, the deeper form, not the 10-day.

questions.q: Does the dip pass the depth rule?
choices: No, it must be 2 ATR or more
No, six days is a long drift
Yes, just: it is at least 1 ATR
Yes, quiet volume is enough
questions.answer: Yes, just: it is at least 1 ATR
questions.why: Yes, just. The depth rule is a close at least 1 ATR under the highest high of the last 11 sessions. 1.01 ATR clears it. MOH was the shallowest of the ten examples, right at the rule's edge. Six sessions also fits the 2 to 8 session length.
questions.lesson_line: One ATR is the line. MOH cleared it by a hair.

wrong.No, it must be 2 ATR or more: The rule is at least 1 ATR, not 2.
wrong.No, six days is a long drift: Two to eight sessions is the length rule, so six fits.
wrong.Yes, quiet volume is enough: Quiet volume is a separate cue. The depth rule asks for a close at least 1 ATR under the highest high of the last 11 sessions.

questions.story: MOH, 2018. Six days sideways on the lowest volume on the chart. The dip is 1.01 ATR deep.
questions.simple: Yes, because the rule needs a dip of at least 1 ATR, and 1.01 ATR just clears it.

deeper.example: MOH dipped 1.01 ATR, right at the 1 ATR edge. Other examples dipped deeper: YELP 1.42 ATR, BFAM 2.24, CAT 2.36. The rule is a minimum, so measure the dip. Do not judge it by eye.

reasons: the 1 ATR minimum is a proposed card number (map.depth)

questions.q: Does a three-day drop fit the length rule?
choices: Yes, 2 to 8 sessions covers it
No, it needs at least 5 sessions
No, a drop is never a pullback
Yes, the 50-day has no length rule
questions.answer: Yes, 2 to 8 sessions covers it
questions.why: Yes. The pullback lasts 2 to 8 sessions from the swing high to the touch day, and three days fits. The drop must also be orderly, with no single down day larger than 2 ATR. BFAM's dip was 2.24 ATR, past the 1 ATR minimum.
questions.lesson_line: Two to eight sessions, and three counts.

wrong.No, it needs at least 5 sessions: The rule is 2 to 8 sessions, so three fits.
wrong.No, a drop is never a pullback: A short, orderly drop onto a rising line fits if no day is over 2 ATR.
wrong.Yes, the 50-day has no length rule: The 2 to 8 session length applies on this card whichever line the stock touches.

questions.story: BFAM, 2019. A three-day drop onto the rising 50 SMA in a steady grinder. The dip is 2.24 ATR deep.
questions.simple: Yes, because the pullback rule is 2 to 8 sessions, and three sessions is inside that.

deeper.counter: Three days is enough, but the drop still has to be orderly, with no single down day larger than 2 ATR, and at least 1 ATR deep. BFAM was 2.24 ATR deep onto a rising 50 SMA.

reasons: the 2 to 8 session length is a proposed card number (map.length)

questions.q: What should you do with this pullback?
choices: Buy; it dipped and came back
Skip it; it slices the line
Call it a Remount and wait
Buy, but with a wider stop
questions.answer: Skip it; it slices the line
questions.why: Skip it. A third close under the line in the same pullback means the name keeps slicing the line. A pullback allows at most two closes under it, the second reclaimed at once. With fewer than 5 closes it is not a Remount either, so there is nothing to buy.
questions.lesson_line: Three closes under the line is a line sliced, not held.

wrong.Buy; it dipped and came back: A third close under the line in the same pullback is a skip.
wrong.Call it a Remount and wait: Fewer than 5 closes under, so it is not a Remount either.
wrong.Buy, but with a wider stop: A wider stop does not fix a line that keeps slicing. A third close under the line in the same pullback is a skip.

questions.story: ADI, 2023. In an 8-session pullback the stock closed under the moving average it was testing three times.
questions.simple: Skip it, because a third close under the line in one pullback means the stock keeps slicing the line.

deeper.trap: Count closes, not feelings. ADI closed under its line 3 times in an 8-session pullback. That is more than a pullback allows and fewer than the 5 closes a Remount needs. In between, the line was sliced, not held.

questions.q: Which check fails on this card?

The distance from the high
The length of the pullback
The volume on the pullback days

questions.lesson_line: Ten sessions is too long for this card. Judge it on the 20 EMA card.

wrong.The distance from the high: That check passes here. The length is the one that fails.
wrong.Whether the line is still rising: That check passes here. Exactly one check fails, and it is the length.
wrong.The volume on the pullback days: That check passes here. The length is the one that fails.

questions.story: META, 2026. A stock drifts 10 sessions from the swing high to its touch day. Every other check on the card passes.
questions.simple: The pullback took 10 sessions but this card allows 2 to 8. A 10-session drift is judged on the 20 EMA Pullback card.

deeper.trap: A near-miss is not a rejection of the stock. The same 10-session drift that fails this card sits inside the 20 EMA Pullback card's 2 to 15 window. Ask which card it belongs to, not whether to throw it away.

questions.q: Which check fails?
choices: Near the 52-week high
The length of the dip
The 10-day line is rising
The volume on the dip days

questions.lesson_line: A stock far under its high is recovering, not leading.

wrong.The length of the dip: That check passes here. Exactly one check fails, and it is the distance from the high.
wrong.The 10-day line is rising: That check passes here. The distance from the 52-week high is what fails.
wrong.The volume on the dip days: Volume is not what fails here. Exactly one check fails, and it is the distance from the 52-week high.

questions.story: AMD, 2019. A dip touches its 10-day on the hold day. The 52-week high is 34.14 and the close is 32.7% under it.
questions.simple: The stock is 32.7 percent under its 52-week high, and a leader must be within 25 percent.

deeper.trap: Do not let a rising 10-day talk you in. The line can be right and the stock still fails the leader test. Here the close is 32.7% under the high, and the card allows 25%.

questions.q: Is this a pullback to buy?
choices: Yes, it just tests the 50-day
No, a heavy close under the line
Yes, if it reclaims it tomorrow
No, the 50-day is too deep

questions.why: No. A close under the line on more than 1.5 times the 50-day volume is distribution, not a pullback. This close came on 4.5 times, far past that. The card drops it before entry, and a reclaim tomorrow does not bring it back.
questions.lesson_line: A heavy close under the line is selling. Skip it.

wrong.Yes, it just tests the 50-day: A close under the line on more than 1.5 times the 50-day volume is distribution.
wrong.Yes, if it reclaims it tomorrow: The card drops it before entry. Heavy selling is not a pullback.
wrong.No, the 50-day is too deep: This card does buy the 50-day, when the low reaches it with the 200-day far below. The heavy close is the problem, not the line.

questions.story: TSM, 2025. A stock sits on its 50-day, then closes under it on 4.5 times its 50-day volume.
questions.simple: No. A close under the line on more than 1.5 times the 50-day volume is selling, not a pullback.

Buy again at once at the same price
Take it; re-enter on a new trigger
Drop the setup; the loss proves it fails

wrong.Move the stop down and wait it out: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.

choices: A normal cost of following the plan
We should have waited one more day
The stop was set too tight to survive
A 50-day buy is not allowed here

A loss taken at the stop is the system working.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out with every rule followed is a normal cost.

choices: 3 in a week and 6 in a month
2 in a week and 4 in a month
1 try, then drop the name for good
No cap if each try triggers anew

questions.lesson_line: Same stock: at most 3 tries a week, 6 a month.

wrong.2 in a week and 4 in a month: The cap is 3 in a week and 6 in a month.
wrong.1 try, then drop the name for good: A stop-out does not end the name. A new trigger starts a new trade, inside the cap.
wrong.No cap if each try triggers anew: There is a cap: at most 3 tries a week and 6 a month on the same stock.

questions.story: PLTR, 2025. Bought at 127.78 on a 10-day pullback, stop 124.27, hit on day 1. It was a one-day shakeout and it climbed later without us.
questions.simple: At most 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock. Each one is a new trade.

deeper.trap: Hindsight says PLTR came back, so the shakeout looks like a gift. On the day, the stop was hit. The plan treats that as new information: the next buy needs its own trigger, its own stop and every rule again.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Get out now and accept the loss
Wait for a bounce to the old stop
Move the stop to the day's low so far
Buy more to lower the average cost
questions.answer: Get out now and accept the loss
questions.why: Get out. After a gap against the stop, the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop. But if those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, the plan is to exit. There are no adds.
questions.lesson_line: Gap through the stop: first 30 minutes decide, past 2R you are out.

wrong.Wait for a bounce to the old stop: The first 30 minutes decide, and past 2R we are out. We do not wait for a bounce.
wrong.Move the stop to the day's low so far: The first 30-minute low is the new stop only when the loss is not past 2R. Past 2R the plan exits.
wrong.Buy more to lower the average cost: No adds. It is one entry at one price with one stop, and averaging down into a gap is not the plan.

questions.story: You hold a pullback buy. It gaps down through your stop. After the first half hour you are down 2.5R on the trade.
questions.simple: Get out, because the first 30 minutes already took the loss past 2R, and the plan exits there.

deeper.trap: Two rules meet here. The new stop is the low of the first 30-minute bar. But if those first 30 minutes already take the loss past 2R, you do not wait for a new stop. You get out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20 and the 2R exit)
fixed before

questions.q: Pullback to buy, or something else?

A pullback; it is inside 25% of the high
A pullback; a first touch is best
A correction; any dip over 3 ATR is one

questions.lesson_line: First touch of a flat 50-day on a broken leader is not a pullback.

wrong.A pullback; it is inside 25% of the high: Inside 25% is only one check. The 50-day is flat.
wrong.A pullback; a first touch is best: A broken leader's first touch of the 50 is a correction.
wrong.A correction; any dip over 3 ATR is one: The card calls a broken leader's first touch of the 50 a correction. Depth alone is not the rule.

questions.story: TSLA, 2024. A former leader is 20.6% off its high, with a flat 50 SMA. The pullback is 3.6 ATR deep and it touches the 50-day for the first time.
questions.simple: It is a correction, because a broken leader's first touch of a flat 50-day is not a pullback.

deeper.trap: TSLA was 20.6% off its high, inside the 25% limit, so it passed that check. The trap is stopping there. Its 50 SMA was flat, the 200 was rising into it, and the dip was 3.6 ATR deep. A broken leader's first touch of the 50 is a correction.

fixed before: the story now says a former leader

questions.q: What does the 5.9% stop mean for the trade?
choices: Nothing; the chart is clean
Size down a lot, or skip
Move the stop up to 3%

questions.lesson_line: A very wide stop means a very small size, or no trade.

choices: Hold; the stop has not been hit
Sell it and free the money
Sell half and trail the rest
Wait for 3R, then reassess

questions.why: Sell it and free the money. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold. The stop not being hit, or the line not breaking, does not change that. The whole trade is sold, not half of it.
questions.lesson_line: Ten trading days under 1R, and the money moves on.

wrong.Hold; the stop has not been hit: A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, even if the stop has not been hit.
wrong.Sell half and trail the rest: The time stop sells the trade. It does not call for keeping half.
wrong.Wait for 3R, then reassess: The time stop is 10 trading days under 1R. It does not wait for 3R.

questions.story: You bought a pullback 10 trading days ago. The trade has not reached 1R of profit. The line has not broken.
questions.simple: Sell it, because a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold to free the money.

deeper.trap: The stop is not the only exit. A trade can stay above the stop and still fail the clock. Still under 1R after 10 trading days, it is sold, even if the line has not broken.

rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before the buy trades. Take this pullback or pass?
choices: Take it; a calm dip held its line
Take it; the stock is just on the line
Pass; the average is falling away
Pass; the dip is too shallow to count
questions.answer: Take it; a calm dip held its line
questions.why: Take it. A stock that had ridden its 10 EMA since February drifted four quiet days onto the line. The dip was 1.42 ATR deep, past the 1 ATR minimum. The touch day ran on only 0.60x volume. 3R came the day after the buy. A clean read is not a promise of the result.
questions.lesson_line: Rising line, quiet dip, a hold. That is the picture.

wrong.Take it; the stock is just on the line: Buying the touch only because it is the line is a card mistake. The reason here is a calm dip and a close at or above the line.
wrong.Pass; the average is falling away: Look again: the line is rising and price has ridden it.
wrong.Pass; the dip is too shallow to count: The dip was 1.42 ATR, past the 1 ATR minimum.

questions.simple: Take it. A stock drifted four quiet days onto its rising 10 EMA and held, which is the picture we want.

deeper.trap: Hindsight makes this easy, since 3R came the day after the buy. The day before, the test is the checklist. Look for a rising line, a dip of at least 1 ATR, quiet volume and a close at or above the line.

reasons: +2 ties to held decision D-003 (the buy over the hold day's high is the default, not a ruling)

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before a would-be buy. Is this a leader's pullback? Take it or pass.
choices: Take it; the dip hit the 10-day
Pass; it sits far under its high
Pass; the dip is too short
Take it; volume fell on the dip
questions.answer: Pass; it sits far under its high
questions.why: Pass. At the hold day the stock sat 32.7% under its 52-week high of 34.14, and the card allows 25%. Only that one gate check fails. It is a recovering stock's 10-day, not a leader's pullback.
questions.lesson_line: A rising 10-day under a deep hole is a recovery, not a leader.

wrong.Take it; the dip hit the 10-day: A touch of the line is not enough. The stock is too far from its 52-week high.
wrong.Pass; the dip is too short: That check passes here. The distance from the high is what fails.
wrong.Take it; volume fell on the dip: Quiet volume does not fix the distance from the high. The card still wants price within 25% of it.

questions.simple: Pass, because the stock sits 32.7 percent under its 52-week high and a leader must be within 25 percent.

deeper.trap: A clean touch of a rising 10-day can fool you. The first question is whether this is a leader at all. Price must be within 25% of its 52-week high, and this stock was 32.7% under 34.14. A bounce from a deep hole is a recovery.

reasons: the 25% limit is a card proposal and a different cutoff was floated
number could change with the owner's ruling

questions.q: Decide which line a stock respects before the trade, not after the low shows where it stopped.
questions.answer: True

questions.lesson_line: Pick the line before the trade. Never after the low shows where it stopped.
questions.simple: True. Choosing the line after the fact is a listed mistake, so decide the line before the trade.

deeper.trap: Once the low is on the chart, you can pick whichever average fits it. That is hindsight, not a plan. Decide before the trade which line this stock respects, then wait for it.

questions.q: How do you answer?
choices: No; size by the stop, not a win rate
He is right; most pullbacks win
Skip the setup; 27.7% is too low
Size up; the test proves our exact edge
questions.answer: No; size by the stop, not a win rate
questions.why: No. Size comes from the stop and the risk rules, and a claim about winning never raises risk past them. In the test of 60,464 hits, 27.7% reached 3R before the stop and 17.5% reached 5R. That is about one in four and one in six, not a high hit rate. The test used a fixed stop with no trims, so it does not measure our plan.
questions.lesson_line: Never size up on a win-rate claim. Size comes from the stop and the rules.

wrong.He is right; most pullbacks win: The test cannot back that. It shows about one in four reached 3R before the stop, which is not a high hit rate.
wrong.Skip the setup; 27.7% is too low: A low hit rate alone is not a reason to skip. The test used a fixed stop with no trims, so it does not measure our plan.
wrong.Size up; the test proves our exact edge: The test used a fixed stop with no trims, so it cannot prove an exact edge for our plan. Size still comes from the stop.

questions.story: A friend says this setup wins most of the time, so size up. Our test of 60,464 pullbacks found 27.7% reached 3R before the stop.
questions.simple: We size from the stop and the risk rules, and a win-rate claim never raises them. Only about one in four hit 3R.

deeper.counter: Two tempting readings are both wrong. 'Most pullbacks win' is not backed by the test: only 27.7% reached 3R before the stop. 'Skip it, 27.7% is low' ignores that the test used a fixed stop with no trims, so it does not measure our plan. The setup's edge is the one-in-four chance of 3R and one-in-six chance of 5R, not a high hit rate.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D45)
the scan numbers can change with new data
fixed before

questions.q: What does the plan do with the last third?
choices: Hold; the trail sells on a close below
Sell now; it broke the 10-day line
Hold, but trail under the 21-day instead
Add back the thirds you already sold
questions.answer: Hold; the trail sells on a close below
questions.why: Hold. The last third of a fast mover is trailed under the 10-day and sold on a close below it. Today closed above the line, so nothing is sold. A dip under it during the day does not count.
questions.lesson_line: The last third rides the trail and leaves on a close below it, not on a dip.

wrong.Sell now; it broke the 10-day line: The sale comes on a close below the line, not on a dip under it during the day.
wrong.Hold, but trail under the 21-day instead: A fast mover is trailed under the 10-day. The 21-day is for steadier movers.
wrong.Add back the thirds you already sold: No adds. The plan trails the last third and sells it on a close below the line.

questions.story: A fast mover you bought has run well past 5R, and you have sold two thirds on the way up. Today it trades under the 10-day at midday, then finishes the day above it.
questions.simple: Hold, because the last third is sold on a close below the 10-day, and today closed above it.

deeper.trap: The trap is selling on the dip. The line is judged on the close. Today it closed above the 10-day, so the last third stays.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51 is adjustable, E52)

questions.simple: True, because our card turns Minervini's one month of a rising 200-day into 21 sessions.

choices: Pass; the 200-day is not rising
Pass; four days is too short a dip
Take it; price is above the 200-day
Take it; four quiet days is clean
questions.answer: Pass; the 200-day is not rising

wrong.Take it; price is above the 200-day: Above the 200-day is the floor. Our card also wants it rising for at least 21 sessions.

choices: Buy 4,000 shares with the same stop
Buy 6,000 with the same stop
Buy 5,000 with the same stop
Skip it; the cap is too small

questions.lesson_line: The stop sizes the trade and the volume cap limits it. Stay under both.

wrong.Buy 6,000 with the same stop: The stop gives 6,000, but that is over 1% of the average daily volume. The cap wins.
wrong.Buy 5,000 with the same stop: 5,000 is still over the cap. The limit is not something to average.
wrong.Skip it; the cap is too small: The cap sets the most you can own. It trims the size and does not cancel the trade.

questions.story: A thin leader averages 400,000 shares a day. Your stop and risk size work out to 6,000 shares.
questions.simple: Buy 4,000, because we never own more than 1 percent of average daily volume, even when the stop allows 6,000.

deeper.trap: Two limits apply at once: the stop allows 6,000 and the volume cap allows 4,000. Both must hold, so the smaller wins. Do not average them, and do not treat the cap as a target.

Week one only; week two is a skip

questions.q: What was missing from the plan?
choices: A real stop order with the broker
A tighter stop, nearer the entry
A price alert on the phone at 30.67
A smaller size to cap the loss
questions.answer: A real stop order with the broker
questions.why: A real stop order with the broker. Every position has one, not a stop kept in your head. A price alert only tells you; it does not sell. Without the order, nothing sold at 30.67 while you were on a call.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is an order with the broker, not a number in your head.

wrong.A tighter stop, nearer the entry: Distance was not the problem. Nothing was in place to sell at 30.67.
wrong.A price alert on the phone at 30.67: An alert only tells you. It does not sell. The stop has to be an order.
wrong.A smaller size to cap the loss: Size already comes from the stop, so size was not what failed. Nothing was in place to sell when the stock traded through 30.67.

questions.story: You buy a pullback at 31.80 and plan to sell if it trades under 30.67. At 2 pm you are on a call and the stock trades 29.90.
questions.simple: A real stop order with the broker was missing, because a plan in your head cannot sell when you are away.

deeper.trap: An alert feels like protection, but it only tells you. At 2 pm on a call you would see it late, and the price may already be through the level. Only an order with the broker acts without you.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41, a live stop order with the broker)

questions.q: If a pullback needs more room, you can move the stop lower to keep the trade open.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. Needing room is no reason to lower it. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. A gap against the stop has its own rule: the low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
questions.lesson_line: The stop only moves up. Never lower it to keep a trade alive.
questions.simple: False, because the stop is the exit and only moves up. Moving it lower for room is not allowed.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop only moves up)

questions.q: By default, when does the stop move to breakeven?

Right after the fill, at the entry
As soon as the trade is up 1R
Once the last third starts to trail

questions.why: When the first third comes off. Our rule moves the stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default. The first trim is a third at 3R, so the default lands at 3R, inside that window.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, by default at the first trim.

wrong.Right after the fill, at the entry: That is not the rule. Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R.
wrong.As soon as the trade is up 1R: 1R is under the window. Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R.
wrong.Once the last third starts to trail: That is after the 5R trim. The default is the first trim.

questions.simple: By default the stop moves to breakeven at the first trim, and that must land between 2R and 5R.

questions.q: Bought at 50.00 with the stop at 48.00. At what price is 2R, where the breakeven window opens?

questions.q: Complete the trim rule.
questions.sentence: A stock gaps up past your 5R level. You take that trim at the ___.
questions.answer: open
questions.why: Open. If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open. The level is already behind you, so the plan does not wait for a pullback to it or for the close.
questions.lesson_line: If it gaps over your trim level, take the trim at the open.
questions.simple: Take the trim at the open, since the stock already opened above your level.

reasons: the key rests on one cited fact (F63)
rests on the owner's rulebook
fixed before

questions.q: How do you handle the first trim?
choices: Take the first third at the open
Wait for it to fall back to 35.19
Take the first third at the close
Wait out the first 30-minute bar
questions.answer: Take the first third at the open
questions.why: Take the first third at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, 3R or 5R, take that trim at the open. The 3R level was 35.19 and the open is 36.40, so the trim is due now. The 30-minute rule is only for a gap against the stop.
questions.lesson_line: The open is above your level. Take the trim there.

wrong.Wait for it to fall back to 35.19: The level is already passed. The rule takes the trim at the open.
wrong.Take the first third at the close: The rule takes the trim at the open, not later in the day.
wrong.Wait out the first 30-minute bar: The 30-minute rule is for a gap against the stop. Above a trim level, the trim comes at the open.

questions.story: Your first trim level is 3R at 35.19. The stock opens at 36.40, above the level.
questions.simple: Take the first third at the open, because the stock opened above the 3R level and the rule is to trim there.

deeper.example: The open can be better than your level. Here 3R was 35.19 and the stock opened at 36.40, so the third sells at the open, not at 35.19. The rule takes the trim where the stock opens.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63, take the trim at the open)

questions.q: What fits our climax rule?
choices: Sell a big part into the burst
Add at the gap; the leg is strong
Hold it all and trail the 21-day
Sell a third, as the trim plan says
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the burst
questions.why: Sell a big part into the burst. On a climax run in your own long, our rule is to sell a big part into it. How much is a judgment call. No adds: the plan is one entry at one price.
questions.lesson_line: Into a climax run, sell a big part. How much is your call.

wrong.Add at the gap; the leg is strong: No adds. A climax is where we sell, not where we buy more.
wrong.Hold it all and trail the 21-day: The rule is to sell a big part into a climax, not to wait for the trail.
wrong.Sell a third, as the trim plan says: The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third. The climax rule is separate: sell a big part into the burst.

questions.story: Your pullback buy has run four days and is still short of 3R. It gapped up twice on rising volume, and today it gaps up again on its widest range yet.
questions.simple: Sell a big part into the burst, because on a climax run in your own long we sell into strength.

deeper.trap: Selling a big part is not selling everything, and how much is your call. Adding because the run looks strong is the opposite of the rule: the plan is one entry at one price, no adds.

reasons: one cited fact only (C34)
rests on the owner's rulebook, whose answer was 'yes but depends'

questions.q: Do you buy the break of the hold day's high?
choices: No; the 20 EMA is under the 50
No; five days is too long a drift
Yes; quiet volume is what matters
Yes; the hold day closed on the line
questions.answer: No; the 20 EMA is under the 50
questions.why: No. The card wants the 20 EMA above the 50 SMA, and here it is under. A 20 EMA that crosses under the 50 SMA takes the pullback off the list. Quiet days and a close on the line do not fix that.
questions.lesson_line: If the 20 EMA slips under the 50, the pullback is off the list.

wrong.No; five days is too long a drift: Five sessions fits the 2 to 8 session length. The averages are the problem.
wrong.Yes; quiet volume is what matters: Quiet volume does not fix the order of the averages. Our card wants the 20 EMA above the 50 SMA.
wrong.Yes; the hold day closed on the line: A hold day alone is not enough. A 20 EMA under the 50 SMA takes the pullback off the list.

questions.story: A leader pulls back five quiet days to its 50 SMA. The hold day closes on the line, and the 20 EMA reads 118.40 against a 50 SMA of 118.90.
questions.simple: No, because the 20 EMA is under the 50 SMA, and that takes the pullback off the list before entry.

reasons: the moving average order test is a proposed card criterion (map.inv_line_flat)
fixed before: the line in the story was changed to the 50-day

questions.q: What does ATR measure?
choices: How volatile the stock has been
Which way the trend points
How heavy the volume has been
How far it sits from its high
questions.answer: How volatile the stock has been
questions.why: ATR measures volatility, gaps included. It does not show direction.
questions.lesson_line: ATR measures how volatile a stock has been, not its direction.
questions.simple: ATR measures how volatile the stock has been, not which way it is going.

wrong.Which way the trend points: ATR does not indicate price direction, just volatility.
wrong.How far it sits from its high: That is a distance off the high. ATR is an indicator of volatility.

reasons: fills the gap that ATR is used in every depth, touch and orderly rule but was never defined

questions.story: You bought a pullback on Monday. Your 5R level is 42.50. News hits overnight, and on Thursday, day 4, the stock opens at 43.10.
questions.q: What fits our plan at the open?
choices: Weigh selling some into the gap
Sell the second third; 5R is a rule
Sell everything left at the open
Add shares because it gapped up
questions.answer: Weigh selling some into the gap
questions.why: Weigh selling some into the gap. A gap past a trim level is not an automatic sell. Selling part at the open is one choice you may make by judgment, never a rule. Day 4 of a push is also a fair time for a first sell.
questions.lesson_line: A gap over a trim level is a time to weigh a sale, not a rule.

wrong.Sell everything left at the open: The plan sells in parts and trails the rest. It does not exit on a gap.
wrong.Sell the second third; 5R is a rule: No trim level is a rule. The first sell is a judgment, and a gap does not force it.
wrong.Add shares because it gapped up: No adds. The plan is one entry at one price with one stop.

questions.simple: Weigh selling some into the gap, because a gap past a trim level never forces a sale and the sale is a judgment.

deeper.trap: A gap past a trim level feels like an order to sell. It is not. Selling part at the open is one choice you may make, and holding the rest on the trail is another.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63, take the trim at the open; E51, a third at 5R)
